Run payroll and HR yourself or have Asure’s experts manage it
Running payroll and HR yourself or having Asure’s experts manage it changes who does the work each pay period. It does not change who the employer is. With either option, the business remains the employer and keeps control of workforce decisions. The choice turns on your team’s time, your in-house skills and the shape of your workforce.
What stays with the employer either way?
The IRS says an employer that outsources payroll and related tax duties to a third-party payer will generally remain responsible for those duties, including liability for the taxes, with an exception for certified professional employer organizations (CPEOs) (Publication 15).


Generally, if the third party fails to perform a required action, the employer remains responsible for the returns, deposits and payments, and the IRS may assess penalties and interest on the employer’s account (Publication 15). The IRS General Instructions for Forms W-2 and W-3 also say that using a reporting agent or other third-party payroll service provider does not relieve an employer of ensuring that employees receive Forms W-2 and that Forms W-2 and W-3 reach the Social Security Administration correctly and on time.


The IRS page on employment taxes and the Trust Fund Recovery Penalty also says the penalty, equal to the unpaid income tax withheld plus the employee share of Social Security and Medicare taxes, can reach any responsible person who willfully fails to pay, including responsible parties within the client of a payroll service provider or professional employer organization (PEO).
What can a provider do on your behalf?
The IRS lists what an outside payer can execute for an employer. A payroll service provider can prepare paychecks and returns for the employer’s signature, make federal tax deposits and payments, and prepare Forms W-2. A reporting agent, authorized on Form 8655, signs and generally e-files returns for each client and may deposit and pay on the client’s behalf. The IRS says neither a payroll service provider nor a reporting agent is liable as an employer or an agent for the employer’s employment taxes (Publication 15 and IRS third party arrangement chart).


AsureWorks is Asure’s managed service, and its specialists run payroll, including payroll tax filing and reporting, and handle day-to-day HR administration. With AsureWorks, Asure specialists do the work on AsureCentral and the client remains the employer, with statutory liability staying with the employer, which matches the IRS’s general rule that an employer who outsources payroll duties will generally remain responsible for them.
How do you stay close to your own account?
For an employer that uses a payroll service provider or reporting agent, the IRS says the employer should activate and use its Inquiry PIN for EFTPS, the Department of the Treasury’s system for federal tax deposits, to monitor its account and ensure the provider is making the required deposits. A reporting agent must use EFTPS to make federal tax deposits on an employer’s behalf, so the employer can confirm in EFTPS that those deposits were made (Publication 15).


The picture differs for a CPEO. A CPEO files aggregate returns under its own EIN, and customers cannot view its deposits in EFTPS (IRS, CPEO customers).


The IRS also strongly recommends that an employer keep its own address as its address of record with the IRS, because IRS notices go to that address. Form 8822-B updates it (Publication 15).
Who decides what the work is?
The IRS common-law test looks at control. A business is the employer when it can control what work is done and how it is done, even if it gives the worker freedom of action (IRS, Employee (common-law employee)). In its guidance on arrangements with a PEO, the IRS asks whether the client directs day-to-day duties, keeps the authority to hire and fire, and sets pay (Internal Revenue Manual 5.1.24).


Those control decisions are worth keeping in view before you hand any work to a provider.
How do you choose between running it yourself and having Asure’s experts manage it?
AsureCentral is a unified payroll and HR platform with one login and shared data, for employers that want to manage payroll and HR internally, and it works best when there is an internal payroll administrator or HR generalist. Asure is not a co-employment PEO. With AsureWorks, Asure specialists can run payroll and handle day-to-day HR administration, but you remain the employer of record and keep control of workforce decisions.


Five checks on your own business point toward the way of working that fits.


* Name who runs payroll and HR today, and who covers when that person is out.
* Measure the hours payroll and HR administration take each pay period, and what those hours would go to otherwise.
* Count the states where you pay employees.
* Check how many employees are hourly and how their time is captured.
* Assess the compliance exposure you carry and who on staff can answer an agency notice or a policy question.
Which questions belong in writing?
The IRS says liability is set by the Internal Revenue Code and cannot be changed by a private agreement or contract (Internal Revenue Manual 5.1.24). A written agreement can still record who does the work and what you can see.


The IRS compares four arrangements by the form filed: none for a payroll service provider, Form 8655 for a reporting agent, Form 2678 for a section 3504 agent and Form 8973 for a CPEO (IRS third party arrangement chart). The IRS publishes a list of certified CPEOs, updated quarterly, and separate lists of suspended and revoked CPEOs.


Ask any provider you consider these questions in writing before you sign.


* Is the provider a CPEO on the IRS list, and what exact legal name and EIN appear in the contract?
* Under whose EIN will Forms 941, 940, W-2 and W-3 be filed?
* Which IRS forms will be on file for us, Form 8655, Form 2678 or Form 8973?
* If the provider is a reporting agent, will we receive its written statement at the start and at least quarterly?
* How can we verify deposits ourselves, and which address is the IRS address of record?
* What does the base fee cover, which HR and benefits services are in scope, what are the service levels, how long does implementation take, and what fees apply on exit?
Frequently asked questions
If a provider misses a deposit, whose account does the IRS assess?
Generally the employer’s account, where the IRS may assess penalties and interest. Two arrangements work differently on the IRS third party arrangement chart. A section 3504 agent and the employer are jointly liable, and a CPEO is generally solely liable for a customer’s employment taxes, returns, deposits and payments on remuneration it pays to worksite employees covered by its contract, and the IRS says a CPEO and its customer may both be liable for remuneration the CPEO pays to non-worksite employees.
What does a reporting agent have to send me?
A written statement when the contract starts and at least quarterly. The statement says the client remains responsible for timely filing and payment of employment taxes and recommends enrolling in EFTPS, under Revenue Procedure 2012-32.
Where can an employer see its payment history and IRS notices?
An employer’s own IRS Business Tax Account, where it is available for the employer’s type of business, shows payment history and lets the employer read notices and letters from the IRS. An employer can arrange for a payroll service or other third party to make electronic deposits on its behalf. When a third party enrolls an employer in EFTPS, the IRS says the employer should activate and use its Inquiry PIN to monitor its own account (Publication 15).
How long should I keep payroll tax records?
At least four years for employment tax records. Publication 15 tells employers to keep all records of employment taxes for that long.
